Artificial intelligence models, modeled after biological agents, can regulate their awareness by restricting their input from the environment to minimize information overload.  A key consideration here is, can a limited perception of its surroundings by an artificial intelligence be efficiently utilized, and what benefits would it confer to its learning process.  A new method has been developed that encourages an artificial intelligence to closely monitor its interactions with its environment by maximizing the exchange of information between its internal states and the external context.  This informational exchange is quantified as the multi-directional mutual information between the internal representation and external context.  To simplify the optimization of this process, the mutual information is approximated using an entropy-based formulation that can be efficiently back-propagated.  This proposed method is efficient in controlling an agent's focus, and it is shown that it leads to a steady and consistent improvement in performance when compared to alternative attention control techniques that are based on the filtered uncertainties of the internal representation.  It is observed that an artificial intelligence trained using this method is capable of detecting and navigating through complex pathways in a simulated world with interconnected modules, whereas its counterparts that use other methods of attention control are either unable to do so or require significantly longer times to complete the task.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and thus inspired local masking, allowing task-independent predetermined graphs, even with sparsity rates as low as 3\%. We introduce locality-masked RNNs and make several breakthroughs, demonstrating these models match or outperform traditional RNNs without recurrent weights on numerous cognitive tasks, achieve faster training speeds, and exhibit better generalization, all while reducing memory consumption by an order of magnitude. Additionally, we showcase locality-masked networks outperform transformer baselines on the GLUE benchmark, opening doors for biological plausibility in high-stakes tasks.

We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we demonstrate how these results contribute to an understanding of the length of anticommutative algebras in further study.

Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence both the black hole's growth and its surroundings in the host galaxy. This research focuses on the effects of a black hole feeding on gas through an accretion disc and emits radiation, while also launching relativistic jets that interact with surrounding dense environments. For the first time, we take into account how cosmic microwave background radiation impacts the formation of these structures, which in turn affects the radio signals we observe. By simulations, we found that at a redshift of 6, the power of these jets is about 10 to 100 times higher than at z=6 from other sources, and we observe radio signals only when the jets have a power above a certain threshold. This leads to a lower density of radio-loud active galactic nuclei at this redshift than previously predicted. Moreover, we found that the growth of black holes is affected more strongly by the cosmic background radiation than by the surrounding environment of dust and gas, which is a key finding.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. By examining the resulting
action terms, we address the issues related to initial conditions, focusing on
regularization and selection of the first order action terms, which define a
gradient hydrodynamics dynamics for gravitational field. We verified that our
results coincide with the conventional $1/c^2$ expansion, offering an
alternative approach to establish non-relativistic general relativity.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results, making it immune to image inversion and 3D transformations that reverse spatial coordinates, achieving SP-symmetry or SP-invariance. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as a set of independent states accounting for possible reflections, irrespective of image contrast. Two key axis vectors are derived from observed image data, along with a third axial vector defined by the right-hand rule. Adding the sign component to the traditional geometry of local features (location, scale, orientation) generates descriptors that are robust to coordinate and contrast inversions. These enhanced feature properties are integrated into symmetric kernel-based point-wise registration, modeled using binary feature correspondence. Empirical results obtained from experiments using the CEDD descriptor as a contrast pool demonstrate that incorporating SP-symmetry results in registration accuracy superior to the current state-of-the-art 3D SIFT approach.

We've analyzed the data from a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, based on our comprehensive photometry observations taken over 318 days. These observations revealed detailed insights into the binary's behavior and allowed us to refine the time of the mid-eclipse. Using individual filter light curve fittings, we determined the low-mass star components and companion star sizes of the binary, finding the white dwarf has a radius of 0.031 R sun, while its companion has a radius of 0.013 R sun at an angle of 87.7 degrees. Furthermore, based on our most suitable model, we estimated the secondary star temperature to be around 5200 K with an error margin of 100 K. Notably, though no noticeable gravitational wave effects on our system's time were found, it is possible to obtain precise 3 sigma measurement of the orbit's decrease in the following year. In 2023 we will see that this orbit decreases due to gravitational forces, resulting in the time at the middle of the eclipse occurring approximately 8 seconds earlier than anticipated.

In numerous machine learning tasks and engineering applications, global pooling operations have been employed for their effectiveness. Nevertheless, the underlying reasoning for their success remains unclear, with some even regarding them as black box techniques. To shed light on this mystery, a novel perspective using optimal transport theory has been established, which offers a unified framework for global pooling methods. By representing pooling operations as ODT-based mapping, the theoretical model encompasses widely used techniques such as average pooling, max pooling and their filter-based variants. Through the development of a regularized least-squares optimizer, it has been demonstrated that this theoretical model achieves optimal transport solutions approximating the desired mapping. Consequently, a theoretical narrative for the global pooling methods is provided, along with empirical evidence supporting the model's effectiveness.

The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER, Type 2 Seyfert, and composite nuclei corresponds to a rise in spiral host galaxies. These findings contradict the unified model, and suggest that there's a symbiotic relationship between supermassive black holes and galactic bulges. Furthermore, our data indicate that spiral host galaxies with Type 1 Seyfert nuclei predominantly face towards the observer, whereas the distribution of Type 2 Seyfert nuclei orientations aligns with those of star-forming galaxies but does not fully match, and is consistent with a contribution of the galactic disc to the obscuration of the nuclear region, also explaining the observed preference of Type 1 nuclei for elliptical hosts.

This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gauss map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training. Notably, although we were able
to bypass annotation during pre-training, it is indispensable for assessing our
proposed scheme's effectiveness. To validate our findings, we employed the
popular KITTI (outdoor) and NYU-V2 (indoor) benchmarking datasets and also
detailed the benefits and shortcomings of our pre-training protocol in the
context of current state-of-the-art methods for depth estimation and semantic
segmentation.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65.38%. Furthermore, an expert review of 21 professionals showed that 76.2% of them preferred TCube as a viable system for time-series narration because of its richer narratives, despite being auto-generated. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for anyone to reproduce our results and build upon our work.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma \leq 1$. By applying a unique approach based on energy estimates and weighted $L_p$-norms with $p \geq 2$, this research provides an energy estimate that is uniform and non-increasing. This approach also offers insights into the properties of solutions and their dependence on the equation's coefficients. Additionally, this work investigates the ill-posedness of certain hyperbolic equations with coefficients that have a polynomial relationship with $|\ln t|$.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora.

On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 1,000,000+ external resources, substantially enhancing the quality of their responses. While several studies have focused on questions and answers, this study endeavors to offer a more comprehensive understanding by examining both questions and answers in conjunction with these external resources. Through advanced data analysis, we identified patterns and trends related to these shared resources. Specifically, we found that a small portion of links are repeatedly referenced by many users across numerous discussions. Consequently, we have developed a predictive model that identifies promising external resources, likely to be referenced again, utilizing both community-based data and the content of related questions and answers. By leveraging this model, developers and maintainers can target maintenance efforts and updates on popular, repeatedly shared resources to maximize their impact.

Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, specifically comparing a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model with isothermal core to Cold Dark Matter models with/without baryonic feedback. Contrary to some feedback models, which can generate a variety of inner galaxy slopes, the SIDM model consistently produces reliable results across a range of interaction strengths and input energies, making it a reliable theoretical candidate to explain galaxy diversity.

Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.
Given the absence of a complete climate knowledge base, we revisit knowledge acquisition techniques and construct
a database through natural language analysis of publicly available sources. To foster further research and applications,
we will publicly release our climate knowledge base, encompassing the relationships between 825 causes, 965
environmental issues, and 1,644 entities. To illustrate its potential, we demonstrate three applications:
customized news, a climate-aware search engine, and value-driven charity suggestions. By making climate information
more relatable and valuable to individuals, we can raise awareness and encourage individuals to act on their own behalf.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained models and adapting them to new contexts. 
Our proposed method involves reducing the number of similarities between datasets by removing common cases, then using these modified datasets for training. 
Experimental results show that this strategy significantly improves the overall performance of symptom extraction. 
This method can be applied more broadly to other NLP tasks and provides insight into the representation of clinical text in various medical settings and professionals.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the transportation sector remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning, given its relevance to autonomous driving due to its independence from preconditions and the extensive learning potential over a prolonged period of time. Although fully autonomous driving poses significant challenges at present, deep reinforcement learning presents a significant prospect for advancing autonomous driving technology in the future.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across diverse datasets.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing local networks, Grid5000, and PlanetLab's distributed nodes spanning across Europe.

A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation.  By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through further processing. Several numerical demonstrations highlight the performance of this solution strategy.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing the properties of Cantor sets, we establish parameter intervals where these transformations exhibit distinct topological invariants, such as ergodicity, mixing, and the presence of natural extensions.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry down to $SO(N_{F})$. Our findings derive from an ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric theory, specifically with anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking.

Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By utilizing this new approach, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and maintain clarity in how their predictions are made, as demonstrated on real-world data and further validated in simulation studies where it was found to surpass alternative methods in recovering predictive models. Finally, a practical analysis using bike-sharing data highlights the utility of DAC in uncovering valuable new insights.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation.

The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a central control unit. The control unit manages testing procedures while the device under test runs the code being tested and its counterpart simulates the interactions with external peripherals. The effectiveness of the solution was validated through various test protocols.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using modern deep learning techniques, Timeloops is comprised of two components: a system call predictor that determines the next system call a program will make and the desired system call stack that should be present on a program's call stack.

Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for translating between different product space forms and maintain linear classifiers in these environments.
Then, we demonstrate a method for converting any linear classifier in a specific product space form into a compatible classifier in another form, showcasing its potential application through a domain adaptation scenario.
Additionally, we introduce a new algorithm that uses a weighted majority voting strategy to combine predictions from different product space forms, offering flexibility and a simple implementation.
Overall, our approach provides a unified approach to linear classification in complex product space structures with various geometric interpretations, offering potential applications in domain adaptation and related fields.

This introduction focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control methods that account for uncertainty in constraints, illustrated through a linear system under unpredictable conditions. The corresponding Matlab code is also accessible online for reference purposes.

This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. By integrating principles from compressive sensing and statistical learning, we develop a framework for compressive independent component analysis, retaining the benefits of minimal measurement processes. The resulting algorithms excel in their ability to accurately recover results, even with a small number of observations, and exhibit superior performance in learning tasks, according to our experimental findings.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range and resulting in its global exclusion.
We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop an approach incorporating a coherent feedback loop. Furthermore, our findings confirm that both the steady and dynamic states of this system exhibit genuine tripartite entanglement. We utilize the logarithmic negativity to quantify quantum correlations between individual subsystems, as well as genuine tripartite entanglement through a nonzero minimum residual contangle. We investigate experimentally feasible parameters that enable the generation of tripartite entanglement and demonstrate its significant enhancement with coherent feedback by adjusting the beam splitter's reflective parameter. Additionally, the proposed entanglement exhibits robustness against thermal effects, making it a valuable property for quantum technologies.

We've obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq\bar{q}$, $q \to qgg$, $g \to gq\bar{q}$ and $g \to ggg$. The exact expressions are derived within dimensionless QCD and include the results of a specific integral up to its second-order expansion. Additionally, we've evaluated the associated splitting functions. Our results are crucial and necessary for creating subtraction and integrated-subtraction terms in next-to-next-to-next-to leading order cross-section computations.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been introduced and applied to the realm of one-dimensional local rings.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future data demands and addressing D2D communication's significant power consumption. To optimize this hybrid network's efficiency, we develop new frameworks for D2D transmission power, data transfer rates, and the hub's power allocation. Our optimization objectives include total data transmission rates, total power consumption, and a trade-off between them. These optimization problems are complex due to interference from D2D transmissions and the hub. However, by assuming that D2D users only receive data from each other and not from the hub, we create an integer optimization problem that can be efficiently solved. This assumption reduces the complexity of D2D power allocation and data rate allocation. Our approach allows us to provide a reliable connection for D2D users and the hub, while also ensuring that D2D transmissions do not disrupt each other's communication. Our approach is also efficient as it allows us to maximize the spectrum efficiency of D2D transmissions and the hub's data transfer. Our approach finally allows the hub to evenly distribute data to those in need and power to those who require it. Our approach is also realistic as it allows D2D transmissions to share the bandwidth with the hub's data transfer and power

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose models of a specific size will accordingly scale in size.  In other words, for any given number $n$, if the models of $\Phi'$ each have size $m$, then there are $m^{n}$ possible subsets, implying a significant lower bound on model size for $\Phi$.  This scaling property holds not just for finite models but also for countable models, although the exponent may differ.  In contrast, we also provide an example of a sentence, denoted as $\Phi''$, with specific properties, such that the models of $\Phi''$ do not scale in a similar manner for any given number of variables.  Additionally, this study also presents a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'''$, with the property that its models of size $m$ will have size $2^{m}$, but this exponent may not be the largest possible for such a sentence.  Finally, we also consider and discuss the problem regarding determining the largest possible exponent for a given number of variables in a sentence.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically engineered to rectify spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for these designs to enhance resolution and 
anti-aliasing under the TEM's constraints. While the phase plates achieve the 
desired defocus, the inherent symmetry of their electric potential prevents 
effective compensation for the TEM's spherical aberration. Nonetheless, we 
identify a feasible approach for designing an aspherical electrostatic phase plate, 
which could potentially utilize an existing curvature in the TEM's objective lens to 
eliminate its aberration, thereby improving the image resolution.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study focused on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. Our approach began by establishing a recursive relationship for the count formula: $|P_n^{d+1}| = |P_n^d| + 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |P_k^d|$. We then presented two distinct methods to derive an explicit equation for $|P_n^{d}|$, involving the application of generating functions and Faulhaber's formula. Our initial method leveraged the use of generating functions to formulate $|P_n^d| $ as the coefficient of $x^k$ in $(1+x^2)^k$. After simplification using the binomial theorem, we were able to express $|P_n^d| $ as a sum of terms, resulting in the application of Faulhaber's formula to calculate the $x^k$ coefficient of $\frac{1}{1-x^2}$. Our second method involved the calculation of odd and even terms separately, leading to the use of the arctangent function. Both methods were verified by examining the special cases of $d=1$, and the relationship between the dimensionality of the space and the step size. This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We explored how in the GOP model the spacelike transition surface at the classical singularity replaces it. Utilizing transformations in the coordinates, the authors were able to extend the metric to the white hole region, which led to discovering that the structure of the quantum black hole bears resemblance to that of wormholes, with their radii equaling each other. Moreover, the authors found that not only is the throat but also the horizons and event horizons spatially coincident. Based on this extended spacetime structure, the authors were able to derive the governing equation for gravitational perturbations, which led to calculating the quasinormal spectrum of the black hole, which includes magnetic parity scalar, vector and tensor cases. The results show that due to the breaking of isometries, the spectrum of the latter two cases becomes highly degenerate. Furthermore, the analysis of the mass gap indicates that due to the minima in the potential, the mass gap exists in all cases, which signifies the stability of the polymer black hole.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality speech, as speaking styles are influenced by dialogue history, leading to unnatural speech patterns when ignoring context. To address this, a new system called MaskedSpeech is proposed, which incorporates contextual information into speech synthesis using a masking strategy. By selectively concealing unessential speech elements and revealing relevant context, MaskedSpeech is able to produce more detailed and human-like speech. To implement this, a masking neural network and a speech synthesis neural network work in tandem, with the masking network identifying which context to incorporate and which speech elements to conceal. The entire system is trained end-to-end using a combination of masked speech and carriage returns as the target output. Our experiments demonstrate that MaskedSpeech outperforms conventional speech synthesis models, specifically a Tacotron-based system, in speech quality according to mean opinion score and objective evaluation metrics.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks often involve a single data exchange. Utilizing TRFL, a pre-trained image generator, we devised an approach to generate adversarial images. Our approach can evolve quickly, adapt to model adjustments, and produce high-quality malicious images, thereby overcoming previous limitations. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that generating adversarial images is more computationally efficient than previous adversarial attacks. Our findings also suggest that the process of creating malicious images facilitates the development of adversarial samples targeting other forms of machine learning classifiers, such as text classifiers.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations, and the counter-conspiracy theories that exist. Our results confirm that counter-conspiracy theories are equally prevalent as the primary ones. Interestingly, we also discovered that people who do not accept climate change are more likely to share conspiracy theories, but individuals who do accept climate change are more likely to share a specific type of conspiracy theory. Our study implies that addressing climate change communication is complex and requires a nuanced approach that takes into account the diverse range of conspiracy theories.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This study analyzed a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions. It differs from earlier studies which focused solely on dark matter creation accompanied by a top quark pair by also investigating cases where a top quark was present individually. Multiple criteria for selecting data categories that fit the single top quark, top quark pair, and dark matter production were developed. No significant anomalies were discovered beyond the predicted background rates. Cross-section limits were established using the 95% confidence level, ranging between 0.65 and 0.78 fb for the single top quark production, and between 0.32 and 0.35 fb for the top quark pair production, both varying according to the choice of renormalization and factorization scales.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that demonstrates the feasibility of combining multiple treatment instruments with ordered outcomes, we analyze a distinct scenario where the instruments result in treatments that can be arranged in a linear sequence. Notably, one of these treatments is considered inferior. Utilizing a novel application of the monoclonal antibody theory initially proposed by Flawith (2008), we establish that combining multiple treatments yields an identifiable counterfactual outcome. Leveraging this finding, we analyze potential biases arising from utilizing fewer than all available treatments and, in doing so, derive a criterion for selecting the most suitable treatment combination. To further illustrate the proposed approach, we conduct an empirical analysis investigating potential returns to specific field of study and apply three distinct IV methods: combining fields of study (CJS), ranking fields of study (RJS), and the generalized threshold approach (GTA), all of which demonstrate notable consequences for field of study combinations on post-education earnings. Among the three methods, CJS proves to be the most reliable approach and reveals the greatest overall success rate in handling instrument uncertainty.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles. As a result, a huge number of $J/\psi$ decays occur annually, creating favorable conditions to accurately analyze these interactions using precision-tagging of co-produced particles. 
This state-of-the-art technology can facilitate groundbreaking studies of diverse targets and open doors for new particle and nuclear physics applications, such as studying antinucleon-nucleon interaction, properties of strange nucleons and nucleon-like particles, (anti)hyperon-nucleon interaction, exotic light hadrons and more, along with advancing our understanding of hypernuclei, calibration of computational methods in hadronic physics and more.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in mass equalization.  Yet, young stellar groups are frequently composed of more than two stars that are predicted to exist in hierarchical triple systems with a high probability.  We conducted a study aimed at determining the rates at which mass is transferred between the three stars in this type of system and observed that the less massive star in such systems receives the majority of accumulated mass.  This outcome is attributed to interactions during the close approach of the third component, which boost the orbital velocity of the outer stars and, as a result, reduce interactions and exchange between the inner and outer discs.  This past research predicted that in binary systems there would be more mass added to the less massive star than to the more massive one.  We found that in hierarchical triple systems, this trend is reversed, with the less massive star in such systems receiving more mass than the more massive one.  We calculated that the less massive star in such systems receives between 55 and 95 percent more mass than the more massive one, with this variation primarily being a result of different disc sizes.
