Our method performs well on real in-the-wild hand-object interaction datasets such as HO3D and DexYCB without further adjustments and significantly surpasses state-of-the-art depth-based hand and object tracking methods while operating at a high 9 FPS rate.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and degrees, with minimal and predictable errors.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional Guassian Random Field models are shown to be a specialized case of this interference model, where the response model remains consistent across all units. Novel methods are developed to analyze treatment interference under the given framework, focusing on key assumptions driving asymptotic analysis. Importantly, a new test is designed to detect treatment interference, where the null hypothesis represents independent units and the alternative indicates the presence of interfering units within a specified radius of influence. For large sample sizes, the test's performance is evaluated, and a method is proposed to estimate the radius of influence. Finally, simulation studies and real-world data analysis are conducted to examine the proposed detection method's effectiveness.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which may equal and potentially surpass those produced by the star's nuclear reactions early on. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's volume and persist throughout the star's lifetime. This information is then used to assess potential impacts of this process on the cooling of a star in the context of existing constraints on dark matter particles.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has just released its second data release. This release comprises approximately 199,000 separate image sections, but a full weak-lensing map based on these images remains yet to be created. To address this, we introduced ShapePipe, a cutting-edge software tool specifically designed to accurately measure the shapes of galaxies. Using the UNIONS data, ShapePipe generated a comprehensive 14,500 square-degree weak-lensing map at moderate resolution, which serves as the initial step in constructing the UNIONS cosmic map. This public map is accessible through the UNIONS website at https://unions.cfis.ca/. ShapePipe is now accessible for free at https://github.com/pjteimore/ShapePipe.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that an irrational number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and certain other conditions are met, it has been shown that, for a wide array of mod $n$ circles where $n$ ranges over a specific collection of numbers, the rotation sequences based on $\alpha$ and the preimages of the $n$-fold map from the circle's boundary to itself display an even distribution. This distribution not only captures the spirit of the mod $n$ extension of the equidistribution theorem first proposed by Veech, but it also encompasses a number of additional instances, including cases based on continued fractions with periodic patterns and sequences related to the mod $k^n$ circles for $k$ values between $2$ and $k_{0}$ where $k_{0}$ is sufficiently large. Notably, these results can be realized without reference to Veech's original input on the matter which is connected to the study of billiards. Instead, a novel topological framework for analyzing the mod $n$ form of the theorem was developed, one which enables the integration of Veech's original observations on the subject. We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime results in a significant drop in the temperature at which 3D order emerges, causing an increase in the critical temperature when it is optimally adjusted. This results in a temperature range where long-range order and long-wavelength quasi-long-range order coexist, which can be efficiently studied by monitoring the finite-size scaling of the structure factor.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as RightmousE, includes an ultra-violet complete QCD axion model which results in the Higgs mass having a lower bound of approximately 125 GeV, due to the influence of neutrino right-handed neutrinos and QCD dynamics. The dark matter composition in RightmousE comprises a mixture of sterile and axion-like particles, which is further examined using recent galactic positron data and current indirect dark matter detection methods. The model's predictions also detail the decay modes of the lightest axion-like particles, such as into photons or vector dark matter particles, based on the Higgs sector's properties. The possibility of detecting the model's predictions in future experiments such as those studying axion-like particle production in the LHC's forward regions or upcoming axion-like particle searches in fixed target experiments is also evaluated.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The found upper bound is $\mathcal{O}(2^{\omega(m)}\mathrm{poly}(\log m))$, where $\omega(m)$ is the minimum number of multiply operations needed to produce a bit string of length $m$. Notably, this optimizes a previous estimate by Childs and Harrow, who had found $\mathcal{O}(2^{\omega(m)+\log m})$. Similarly, the study enhances the understanding of classically implementing quantum circuits comprising Clifford and $\sqrt{T}$ gates, and sets a maximum limit on the number of stabilizer states needed to express $|H\rangle^{ \otimes m}$. The study also invents a verification-of-classical-circuit scheme, for which the amount of required computation is determined by the number of stabilizer states used to express a given quantum state, and proves it to be secure against quantum adversaries when a certain condition on the computational problem used in the circuit is hard. The study specifically shows that classically simulating $n$-qubit circuits requiring $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$ multiply operations to prepare $|T\rangle$ would solve the problem $B_2^{

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios as real universe descriptions 
by calculating the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two parts 
of the quintessence field effect: the complex and real parts. We assume the real part 
behaves as pressure-less dust, which helps us derive a critical value for the 
fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D} < 0.7$, as obtained from the combined analysis 
of fractional energy density equations.
Furthermore, our assumption that the real part behaves as pressure-less dust 
results in lower values of the fractional energy density, which helps us understand 
the impact of this assumption on the model.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST time-domain survey, which tracks changes in stars, gathered early data on 1,533,691 stars during its initial run. These findings come from four $K$2 plates and involve 216,692 repeated observations of 114,417 stars. The data show that these stars are primarily main sequence objects with minimal evolutionary changes. The research discovered and verified 2,916 variable stars, consisting of DD Harpstar, $\delta$ Scuti, RR Lyrae, and Cepheid variables. The project successfully identified 1,213 new stars, including 1,015 RR Lyrae and 198 Cepheid variables that were previously unknown. To verify these results, the LAMOST time-domain survey's data were cross-checked with other astronomical databases, demonstrating consistency. The accompanying figure shows a sample of variable star light curves. These early findings pave the way for further research and set goals for the LAMOST time-domain survey through BD.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-quality RNG output. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high randomness and long-lasting capacity of TuRaN, thereby serving as a trustworthy TRNG solution.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in certain situations. Our approach mainly relies on the extension theory and the linked Weyl-Titchmarsh function, in addition to standard one-dimensional quantum walks principles.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows. Furthermore, for a specified range of $q$, these systems exhibit amplification of the optical signal. By manipulating parameters like tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, one can cause the optical pulse to be delayed or advanced. This work lays the groundwork for applying $q$-deformation to better understand and manipulate optical phenomena and their applications.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1 components with negative parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that reverse the orientation of these scissors modes, resulting in R-negative states. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflection symmetry and R-symmetry, correlating reflections with R-parity breaking. Consequently, I identified a subset of these reflections as R-negative scissors modes, specifically R-breaking, with collective 1 |K| = 1 and 3 |K| = 1 components. While the collection is R-breaking, only the 1 |K| = 1 component is negative. Calculations using the weak coupling limit revealed that the transition strengths from the 0+2@g J
u=2@g J'=
u' quantum band to these R-breaking scissors modes show strong, gated transitions. Experimental evidence was found, with the most prominent example being a 1578 keV 2+@g J'=2@g J'=
u'=2@g J' resonance in 180Nd.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these fluctuations emerge and demonstrate that the thickness-induced transition is caused by a competition between kinetic energy and on-site Hund's exchange energy. Furthermore, we applied the Bonn-Mersey functional to examine the role of charge and phase fluctuations in the thickness-induced transition. Our findings are consistent with experimental observations and provide a framework for understanding the complex behavior of thin metallic transition-metal oxides.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for distributions characterized by long, power-law tails. One such physical system - laser-cooled atomic ensembles - offers an optimal platform to study such phenomena, primarily due to its distinctive friction force. This interplay between laser cooling and anomalous dynamics is likely to reveal profound and predictive insights into both equilibrium and non-equilibrium statistical physics. In experiments involving cold-atom systems, scientists can manipulate and adjust various system parameters to observe changes in the system's behavior, and this has been achieved by analyzing non-normalized states associated with rare events, utilizing tools derived from infinite ergodic theory, resulting in new findings.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate peaks in significant events, while the corresponding network structure exhibits stability, with most influential nodes being cryptocurrencies. Contrasting with pairwise analysis, stable coins appear in few synergistic connections, but when considering high-order relationships, they dominate synergistic circuits, highlighting their role in higher-order effects. Furthermore, a high volume of total transactions in the US dollar market of a cryptocurrency does not always translate to a higher degree of the trading network, implying non-linear market behavior. The research sheds light on the structure and dynamics of the cryptocurrency market, yet raises concerns regarding the reliability of this investment due to extreme price fluctuations and volatility.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for certain systems. The current research evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water. The findings reveal that its importance depends on the composition of the cluster and potential energy levels of its components. Generally, the incorporation of zero-point motion corrected configurations in large clusters does not substantially deviate from classical-based counterparts but becomes more notable in smaller particles. The discovery that zero-point motion has the potential to transform their composition and thus their physico-chemical properties could influence the overall particle yield and thus the cloud condensation nucleus concentrations.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in compactifying this space.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this thermal analogy does not hold; while an uneven gravitational force induces specific energy flows, a comparable uneven temperature has little to no effect in systems that exchange energy with their surroundings weakly. Additionally, the similarity between an external electric charge and the system's internal energy is also invalid under these circumstances.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity of this method over a likelihood-based approach that divides the phase space into distinct regions.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks and variants like Long Short-Term Memory cells, but more recent studies have successfully applied Transformer architectures and attention-based mechanisms.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of sentence reverse and its combinations with existing transformation methods in enhancing the accuracy of automated essay grading using transformer models.  Notably, our findings indicate that the reverse sentence approach yields a high level of accuracy, surpassing more complex sentence translation methods, while also reducing the complexity of generating training data and model computations.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice may vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through both security proofs and practical evaluation.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of around 3.3 to 3.4 standard deviations and the measured rates of boson creation are also recorded.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus.

We maintain fixed the values of $1 < p < \infty$ and $1 \leq q < \infty$. It is established that for any given $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, an arbitrary subset $A$ of $\ell_p$ and its corresponding subset $B$, which comprises elements with absolute values less than or equal to one, it is possible to find a linear transformation that achieves an $\varepsilon$-isometric distortion on $A$ while also preserving its structure with respect to scaling in $\ell_q$. This result is further illustrated with $\ell_1$ as an example, where it is shown that an incompressible subset $A$ of $\ell_1$ can be represented with a precision of $\varepsilon$ using at most $\frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}}$ consecutive coordinates.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated progress in data-driven modeling but also create new challenges: the scarcity of extensive measurement datasets and the difficulty of selecting reliable output variables. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel cooperative method that bridges data-driven and physics-based modeling approaches. This innovative framework enables the efficient discovery of relevant output variables and allows limited measured data to be extended to the entire domain through collaboration with physically informed models. By leveraging the strengths of both approaches, cooperative models can effectively handle unstable equilibrium solutions and accurately capture oscillatory dynamics in pressure and flow. Furthermore, this framework can reduce the requirement for measured data by up to tenfold while still achieving a high level of accuracy.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection capabilities, posing a significant threat to QKD systems utilizing quantum field amplification. To mitigate this, we propose an improved QKD system design featuring partial phase randomization and multi-channel measurements. However, this novel design renders existing quantum hacking techniques ineffective and significantly diminishes the  attacker's advantage in eavesdropping, thereby protecting the system against linear optics-based hacking. Furthermore, our improved QKD system can function without noticeable distortions in real-world conditions, thereby ensuring secure communication.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora with models of different sizes. Our research aims to explore these questions by analyzing the relationship between the mentioned components, particularly with a 1.3 billion parameter language model, and we find that training corpora and model size significantly affect learning in-context, largely due to the impact on data density and category richness. Moreover, we reveal that learning in-context is often enhanced by incorporating data segments that improve understanding of word meanings, even if these segments contain incorrect labels. Our findings suggest that using diverse, word-rich training corpora is essential for developing models with in-context learning capabilities, particularly with larger models. Additionally, we show that combining multiple corpora can overcome data sparsity issues in smaller models, though the benefits tend to decrease for models of our given scale.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when multiple cold clouds coalesce. To investigate this, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of galaxy cluster core formation, considering various initial cloud distributions, magnetic fields and thermal conduction. Our results indicate that in a 3D realm, a single dominant filamentary structure forms, either from an isolated cool core or by cloud merging, and can either be a cool core or a filamentary feature. When multiple clouds are present, they either pass through or orbit within the primary filamentary structure. Additionally, we found that in a 2D simulation, a hierarchical network of filamentary structures forms, and that magnetic fields and thermal conduction play a significant role in the growth of these structures. However, when considering the role of radiative cooling, we found that in the absence of magnetic fields and thermal conduction, the formation of a hierarchical structure is replaced by a uniform cool core, as the gas collapses in the presence of magnetic fluctuations.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially identified $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and made
the most accurate measurement of this effect within the charm system to date. 
These analyses rely on data gathered from proton-proton collisions in 2011 and
2012, collected by the ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, these networks can efficiently handle complex tasks without overloading the Backhaul networks. This thesis focuses on developing core network management processes for autonomous and self-sustaining 5G networks. It proposes a new model for mobile network core computation resources, and introduces the concepts of resource management processes, including task scheduling, computation resource allocation, and vendor neutrality. Additionally, the thesis develops several optimization techniques for managing resources, and suggests using Self-Organizing Networks (SONs) for decision-making purposes. It also presents a framework for implementing autonomous and self-sustaining networks, and suggests using Machine Learning algorithms to optimize network performance. Finally, the thesis outlines simulation scenarios and suggests future areas of research.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the acoustic units in the training data, and then constructing a synthesis system that can learn from speech data without transcription, by leveraging the definition of acoustic units. Specifically, the unsupervised unit model is integrated with a neural network that performs speech synthesis, and the system's performance is evaluated using the Distinguished Feature Sets task and the unsupervised Diphone Synthesis task. The results indicate that the proposed system outperforms the baseline on both tasks.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between consecutive stages to ensure feasible postures and forces. By introducing specific constraints and using relaxed McCormick envelope predictions, we establish inner and outer bounds for the original nonlinear problem, successfully solving it within a practical time frame. Our proposed framework has been effectively applied to a variety of balanced and unbalanced stance configurations.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution due to quantization. The decentralized change-quadratic regularization issue is redefined and analyzed, and under specific conditions, a distributed optimization algorithm (DR-DSGD) is developed using stochastic graph theory and analysis. The DR-DSGD algorithm is proven to converge deterministically and randomly to an optimal solution, which outperforms existing decentralized optimization methods in robustness, according to theoretical findings. The efficacy of the DR-DSGD algorithm is validated through numerical experiments on various graph topologies.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that highly energetic jets only occur under low magnetic field conditions and when a large amount of material is drawn towards the star, leading to elevated internal pressures. These high-velocity jets can then penetrate deep into their surroundings, with the ability to exert pressure on the star's accretion disk. The simulation reveals that for these high-velocity jets to emerge, a significant portion of the total energy must be allocated to them. The results also indicate that the energy from the high-velocity jet is likely to be dissipated as it interacts with the accretion disk, which in turn raises the question of whether this energy can be effectively transferred to a slower-moving outflow. Therefore, it can be hypothesized that the origin of a slower-moving outflow may not be directly linked to a higher-velocity jet.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced control and estimation (BCE). A novel approach involves introducing a satellite mechanism to monitor and adapt to filter and backstepping adjustments, ensuring system stability can be maintained even in the event of extreme filter and backstepping modifications. A balance is struck between performance and system resilience to error fluctuations caused by excessive adjustments. Furthermore, an alternative model with reduced complexity is presented, utilizing a simplified model with a fixed filter to improve system stability and performance. Illustrative simulation examples, involving a vertical takeoff and landing aircraft and a jet aircraft, showcase the efficacy of the proposed strategy in achieving impressive performance enhancements while effectively managing system constraints.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect an object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its shape and the impact of sunlight pressure. To achieve this, it provides mathematical predictions for the object's equilibrium positions, taking into account its area-to-mass ratio, initial conditions, and the object's variations in eccentricity. Estimates are also developed for the time intervals in which these orbital changes occur, which is crucial in categorizing the object's orbit under different influences. Validation of these estimates was conducted through numerical modeling and the application of specialized tools, such as the Fast Lyapunov Indicator, which helps to identify and visualize patterns related to resonance phenomena. Ultimately, this work aims to lay the groundwork for modeling the impact of sunlight pressure in the framework of established celestial mechanics models, specifically the Extended Fundamental Model and the Second Fundamental Model.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models applied to two-dimensional monolayers and quantized thin films. We find that the dipole-based model satisfies the condition for gauge invariance when properly defined, whereas the velocity-based model does not. We develop a statistical approach to quantify the degree of gauge violation, which we utilize to assess the reliability of tight-binding parameters derived from first-principle methods. We also demonstrate that gauge-violating effects are noticeable in certain optical properties when the driving force is strong and the electronic bandstructure is complex. Nevertheless, we contend that the dipole-based model is a more reliable and robust method for modeling light-matter interactions, particularly in scenarios where driving forces are strong.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we aim to accurately identify the pose and shape of objects within specific categories despite variations in appearance and shape. To achieve this, we propose PACE3D, a novel flexible framework that utilizes 2D and 3D semantic keypoints to determine object pose and shape. PACE3D consists of an optimal pose estimator, a reliable shape predictor, and a reliable classification system. Our approach is influenced by decision theory and robust estimation techniques. We evaluate PACE3D using various object datasets and analyze its performance for both robust and non-robust versions. Our results indicate that PACE3D outperforms existing competition methods, showcasing its superiority in object pose and shape estimation. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of PACE3D in autonomous vehicle applications, particularly for object interaction and path planning.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for assessing whether treatment effects differ between patient subsets in basket trials by sharing information between subsets. This method calculates the required sample size for each treatment group by considering hypotheses for each subset and assuming dependency between groups. To facilitate this, our approach uses a Bayesian framework with Laplace-Bernoulli distributions and develops an iterative method to find suitable prior probabilities. These probabilities maximize the likelihood of observing treatment differences between groups, effectively incorporating prior knowledge. We derive closed-form formulas for calculating the required sample size and illustrate our approach using a hypothetical basket trial.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across varying views and objects, while its geometric representation is transferable to classification tasks.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the nilpotency degree of $G/\ker\varphi$ and calculate its upper limit. Furthermore, we classify the nilpotency degrees of nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups. In a particular instance, we derive the Weyl Chern classes of a nilpotent quotient of $BS(2, 3)$.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found, researchers consider a more plausible scenario where various particle colliders will be built to explore multiple possibilities of new physics. Given that findings may be inconsistent across different experiments, we evaluate the potential of forthcoming lepton colliders and other potential facilities to pinpoint the nature of SM instability in the absence of new physics. Compared to current understanding, future high-energy machines will have significantly enhanced sensitivity. While Higgs stability is the primary concern at lower energy colliders, such as the ILC and CLIC, research focuses on the main production mode at higher energy machines like the Future e+e+ e- collider and FCC-ee. These future colliders will be capable of identifying the origin of SM instability, specifically whether it arises from Higgs boson interactions or other processes.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In this study, a Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network is proposed that simultaneously performs domain adaptation and object identification within a single unified structure. Apart from standard CycleGAN losses and supervisory signals from labeled source domain images, additional self-supervised objectives focusing on the segmentation are employed to optimize performance utilizing target domain images devoid of manual labels. Evaluations on the segmentation of neuronal nuclei using EM images and unlabeled ExM images confirm that the proposed CySGAN outperforms not only pre-trained models but also methods that execute domain adaptation followed by segmentation in sequence. Details regarding the model implementation, newly acquired densely annotated ExM dataset called NucExM, are accessible at the specified link.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine learning, including k-NN and RBF kernels, to develop a novel RNN architecture that anticipates future actions. By mapping visual features to a higher-dimensional space, Feature Mapping RNN can utilize the RBF kernel to forecast future states, enabling the design of anticipated motion trajectories. In contrast to prior expectation-maximization-based methods, Feature Mapping RNN optimizes both kernel and parameter objectives, yielding significantly improved action forecasting outcomes. Furthermore, our study highlights the connection between kernel and feature maps, demonstrating that pre-trained kernel models can be converted into motion predicting models with superior performance. Thorough experiments, including AICHI and JHMDB datasets, validate our method's robustness and superiority in action forecasting.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical electron collisional broadening formulas for predicting Lyman lines, which are supplemented with detailed stratification models of metal lines to estimate the photospheric intensity of the stellar flare. Comparison with observed data during the peak of the 1985 April 12 flare of AD Leo shows that the predicted continuum flux matches the observed trend of $F_{\lambda} \propto \lambda^{-1.5}$ in the near-UV to optical spectrum. However, discrepancies remain in the near-UV range at lower flux levels, which may be attributed to underpredicted flux levels by up to an order of magnitude using the current model, which emphasizes the need for space-based near-UV spectroscopy of stellar

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been compromised by outbreaks of false positives and negatives. Researchers have explored various techniques to improve the models' robustness but most are designed to handle specific types of attacks and require comprehensive retraining after adaptation. A new technique called TPC has been developed to provide sophisticated defense mechanisms against multiple types of attacks without the need for model retraining. TPC uses statistical methods to characterize the statistical characteristics of legitimate data and employs decision-based strategies to detect anomalies based on the decisions made by the model itself. Through experiments, it has been demonstrated that TPC can effectively prevent false negatives and reduce false positives on various types of attacks while maintaining the model's accuracy.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease system efficiency. We introduce a clear channel assessment mechanism to enhance the CSMA protocol. To estimate the number of active transmitters, each radar unit gauges the power of its received signal, comparing it to a threshold to determine if the channel is clear or not. We analyze the effectiveness of CSMA and note that it outperforms slotted ALOHA under most conditions. However, CSMA may experience performance degradation if there are many active transmitters and its back-off process becomes inefficient. In some situations, ALOHA can offer better performance than CSMA. We're exploring solutions to optimize medium access in radar networks.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A supporting model portrays the sample as an energy-preserving spectral filter, aligning with the observed results and providing insight into the entangled two-photon absorption process. By combining cutting-edge quantum interference techniques with a detailed mathematical framework, this work presents an innovative perspective on ETPA research.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we present TimeBEE, a low-dimensional representation that generates
temporally-embodied vectors for enhancing temporal knowledge graph completion.
Compared to existing representations, TimeBEE boasts model independence, reduced
training data requirements, and a simpler architecture with fewer trainable parameters.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of TimeBEE through our integration of tensor
decomposition, relational rotation high-order interaction model, high-order hidden
state model, and special temporal knowledge graph completion models, which yield
satisfactory results on various metrics and datasets, including small, medium, and
large scale datasets such as Semantic-MEB, TempAsk, TKG-1033, FDTK, and Google
Knowledge Graph, resulting in consistent performance improvements across these datasets.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface, which is then used to compute the pressure waves reaching a nearby receiver. This calculation involves an integral equation that requires modeling the sound production mechanism. Two plausible mechanisms are presented, one of which involves a frequency-dependent filter and the other, associated with higher frequencies, involves a geometric approximation of the sound production. The model derived from the idealized ground sound theory is compared with experimental results, showing that ground sound can be audible under specific circumstances and its intensity varies significantly with different parameters. Moreover, ground sound can be louder than the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations, counteracting a common assumption that it would be weaker.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without utilizing inequalities. Instead, it relies on perfect correlations that may not exist in practical experiments. However, this paper proposes a modified version of the all-versus-nothing proof that utilizes imperfect correlations still implying Bell nonlocality, thereby making the concept accessible with quantum technology that produces correlations with small errors.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in superconducting bio- or co-doped graphene, caused by chiral symmetry breaking, can be modeled using MOs. Various protocols for generating flat bands are examined along with their implications for localization, before applying the MO model to numerical simulations of conducting zero modes in graphene.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this system with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Ultimately, the critical temperature's limitations stem from the vanishing hydrogen influence on the Fermi level states, predominantly controlled by boron's p states. Consequently, substantial amounts of hydrogen-like states near the Fermi level are essential for attaining significant superconducting critical temperatures in such systems.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here coincidentally relate to the numbers A124324 in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. A distinct counting method is developed for these numbers, and we establish a one-to-one correspondence between a specific type of division and the division of quantities into fewer equal parts. Furthermore, we introduce a set of numbers, $f_{n, k}$, which represent the count of a specific type of division containing $k$ distinct segments. Recursive relationships defining these numbers, along with their differential generating function, are provided. Identifying a closed form expression for these numbers is a desirable outcome. Lastly, we generalize our results to scenarios where the first segment consists of different parts, accompanied by combinatorial evidence.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain higher-level structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain complexity structure, exhibit rigidity as well.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and rely on redundant systems, including automatic emergency braking systems, to guarantee safety. Traditional testing methods are often insufficient, leading automakers to employ formal verification: a mathematical approach that rigorously proves a system's behavior meets specifications, unlike informal proof methods such as FMEA (Failure Mode and Effect Analysis) which provide approximate results. In contrast, formal verification offers precise results, revealing critical system flaws in case of inadequate design. As an advanced application of highly automated driving, we conduct formal verification of a fail-operational automotive driving system and present the results to establish the reliability of such systems in critical situations.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. Current methods for finding communities or clusters in these systems often rely on underlying assumptions that may not always hold true, leading to inaccurate results. In this research, we propose a novel approach called InFlu, which uses dynamic time-warped data to group systems based on influence rather than assuming a specific system structure. By transforming the inverse of the system's discrete-time evolution matrix into a similarity measure, InFlu creates an approximate matrix that captures the connections between systems. Since this approach relies on data rather than a specific model, it's susceptible to noise and the quality of the resulting clusters heavily depends on it. InFlu's time complexity is relatively high, at O(N^2.37), which may become a limitation for large datasets. Nevertheless, InFlu outperforms existing methods in multiple applications, including a massive solar flare dataset with over 10,000 solar flares.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating which of the major real analysis theories it aligns with the most. This study diverges from that line of inquiry, instead striving to comprehend the fundamental principles of Leibnizian calculus. Through an examination of crucial concepts such as continuity, differentiability, and the nature of the infinitesimal, this paper seeks to build an accurate depiction of Leibnizian calculus within the frameworks of informal $\mathbb{R}$-limitology, formal $\mathbb{R}$-limitology, and formal $\mathbb{R}^\d$-limitology. It finds that the $\mathbb{R}$-limitological rendition of Leibnizian calculus offers the most comprehensive depiction of this system.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be dominated by redshift $z \simeq 0.5$, we find that the shot noise dominates the dispersion of the measured power spectrum multipoles and that the linear bias factor significantly impacts the resulting best fit values of cosmological parameters. Accounting for the effects of foregrounds on the measured power spectrum is necessary; specifically, we find that assuming a model with scale-independent amplitudes of HI-related and foreground-related fluctuations that are in ratio with each other, but with different exponents, results in shot noise dominated variance of the measured power spectrum and the best fit values of cosmological parameters that are in agreement with their theoretical values. We found that the constraints on the matter fluctuation amplitude are reduced by a factor of two when comparing to those from the measured power spectrum amplitudes at $z=\text{0.5}$. Additionally, we found that the best fit values of the matter fluctuation slope are consistent with zero. Given that the shot noise dominates the dispersion of the measured power spectrum, we found that the constraints on other parameters are highly uncertain and subject to change when further data is obtained.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account users' perspectives on these items. Additionally, our model offers the advantage of online personalization where the system can adjust the user and item representation profiles upon detecting new user interactions without requiring updates to the model's parameters. Our proposed algorithm was tested and demonstrated superior performance on three real-world datasets when compared to baseline methods.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've demonstrated an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we prove the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We also identify new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ terms exhibiting isospin breaking and that additional isospin breaking arises due to the presence of loops containing kaons, as these do not cancel out when charged and neutral kaon masses differ. A calculated branching ratio for $a_0(980)$ production was found to be on the order of $5 \times 10^{-6}$. It is suggested that forthcoming experiments will have the capability to measure this decay, allowing researchers to place a limit on the $a_0(980)$ yield and thereby test the current understanding of this process. Moreover, studies of several other studies, such as $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta'$, have the potential to be measured with forthcoming experiments, which will have a sensitivity on the order of $10^{-6}$. These studies will have the capacity to verify the prevalence of $
